searches.note: Twenty four searches of a share of twenty eight, four left unspent, none of them the author's. Three were shared by the records that meet John Riddoch (the ADB once, the Coonawarra Vignerons once, the Penola Fruit Colony once with the house domains kept out). Five were restricted to one domain (adb.anu.edu.au twice, coonawarra.org once, wynns.com.au once, majellawines.com.au once, counting the shared ADB search); the rest kept the house's own domain out where the author had leant on it, so that each second source would be independent. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The worktree held an uncommitted third pass of the author's, written by its scratch scripts eleven minutes after the push (Wynns making; Katnook making, ageing, both label terms, story and a card; Parker making, glass, table and a source; Majella making, story and an explanation; Lindeman's grapes). The check read that working copy, which carries every pushed change, and tested each of those fields as it tested the rest; the commit carries them, set right where this check refuted them. They are listed under thirdPass with the pushed text beside them.

History went first to the Australian Dictionary of Biography, the Coonawarra Vignerons and local history (the Yallum Park timeline, the Royal Oak at Penola, a centenary plaque at Katnook, the Paterson Historical Society); the making went to the houses' own notes and to merchants' sheets with the house's domain kept out.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in only one listing that is not the house speaking of itself, it was cut or said with less; the house's own claims are told as its account.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Gourmet on the Road, Chris Shanahan, Campbell Mattinson, Jancis Robinson's) are cited neither in the fragment nor as a second source here. The serving temperatures agree with the service reference: medium reds 15 to 17 for Wynns Black Label, full reds 16 to 18 for the other four.

tested: John Riddoch, 1827 to 1901, bought Yallum near Penola in 1861: the ADB. Confirmed; the story's pastoral run and its dates stand.

The Penola Fruit Colony of 1890: 1,147 acres north of Penola cut into ten and twenty acre lots in 1890 by the Yallum Park timeline, the ballot for blocks held at the Royal Oak in July 1890, and the Coonawarra Vignerons; the ADB's entry for George Riddoch says 1891. Kept at 1890, the open question recorded.
The triple gabled winery: 1896 by the Coonawarra Vignerons, 1897 by Decanter and Good Food, 1891 and 1896 by the house. The record's 1890s stands.

The purchase of 1951 and the renaming: Samuel and David Wynn bought the defunct Chateau Comaum and its vineyards and renamed them Wynns Coonawarra Estate (Wikipedia, the ADB entry for David Wynn, the Coonawarra Vignerons, which add that the Wynns created the gabled label). Confirmed; the family stays undescribed by name, as the author chose.

The first Black Label of 1954 and the count: the 2015 the sixtieth vintage and the 2018 the sixty third (Canterbury Wines and two merchants), which leaves two years without one since 1954. Confirmed: most years, and the house's count.
The vines of the 1950s and 1960s: the house's 2021 note. Confirmed as primary.

The making: the house's notes for 2018 to 2023 give fourteen to fifteen months in French oak, 21 to 31 per cent new, mostly hogsheads with barriques and 6 to 13 per cent in large vats; a 2015 note gives eighteen months; a 2009 listing and house material of about 2017 name American oak beside French, twelve to eighteen months by vintage. Refuted in part and rewritten.
The name Black Label: no source of three searches says where the name came from. The gloss cut.

Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind; the Redman explanation agrees with the Rouge Homme sale of 1965. Rules: no living name, no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. Sound.

tested: The woolshed: erected in 1862 for John Riddoch by the centenary plaque at the estate, 1867 by the house. The 1860s stands.

The vintages of 1895 and 1896: a first, modest vintage in 1895 and the first commercial one in 1896 in the woolshed, made by William Salter the younger, by the plaque, the Coonawarra Vignerons and Wine Selectors. Confirmed; the trained winemaker stays described, since his dates were not found.

The modern estate: the property renamed Katnook Estate and new vines planted in 1971, the first modern vintage of 1980 made in the woolshed (the Coonawarra Vignerons, Wine Selectors). Confirmed; the winemaker of 1980 is living and unnamed.

Odyssey: the 1991 vintage released in 1996 for the centenary of the woolshed vintage, its name for the estate's journey with its roots in the past (Food Wine Travel and two others, with the house domain kept out). Confirmed.

The making: thirty seven months, two thirds in French oak, half of it new, and a third in older American (Decanter China's promotion), thirty six to thirty nine months for 2013 to 2015 by the house. The author's thirty months and more stands; much of it new is said with less.

The barrel room: the woolshed serving as the barrel room is found in a writer's article of 2020 on a mooted sale, which this check may not cite, and it is a present use. Cut from the label and the card.
Questions: one right answer each; the distractor dates (1890, 1971, the GI) are of one kind. Rules: sound.

tested: Henry John Lindeman, 1811 to 1881, born at Egham, trained at St Bartholomew's, qualified in 1834, died at Cawarra on 23 May 1881 (the ADB; an obituary quoted on a family site says 26 May). Confirmed.
The ship's surgeon: surgeon on the Dreadnought hospital ship and to India, then ship's surgeon on the Theresa to Sydney in 1840 (the Paterson Historical Society, a settlers' register). Confirmed.
Cawarra: bought at auction in January 1842 by two family history sites, 1843 by a medical journal; vines planted in 1843 (the ADB and the house). The planting stands; the purchase stays out.

The 1950s and 1965: wine bought for blending in the 1950s (the Coonawarra Vignerons, with Food and Drink Business naming Lindeman's among the buyers of Redman wine in bulk); the Rouge Homme winery, label and vineyards bought in 1965 (Redman's own history, Winetitles). Confirmed.
Limestone Ridge: planted in 1967 or 1967 and 1968, mostly Shiraz with a little Cabernet, named for shallow soil over a ridge of limestone (Canterbury Wines, Langton's, Nick's). The late 1960s stands.
The blend: 60 per cent Shiraz for 1986, 54 for 1994, 83 for 1997, about 78 for 2016 and 80 for 2022. Some three quarters refuted as a rule.

The oak: eighteen months for 2009 in American oak part new, eighteen months in new and seasoned American and French later (Tastingbook, merchants); stainless steel and hogsheads in one listing each. Cut.

The Jimmy Watson Trophy: the St George Cabernet Sauvignon 1980 by Wikipedia (award year 1981), Melbourne Royal's list (in its 1980 row) and a University of Adelaide factsheet. The vintage stands, the award year cut.

thirdPass.pushed: Katnook stands on land that was part of John Riddoch's pastoral holding, and, as the house tells it, Riddoch (1827 to 1901), who had settled near Penola in 1861, commissioned its woolshed, the first building on the site, in 1867. In 1890 he turned part of his land into the Penola Fruit Colony and planted vines, and by the house's account a small first vintage in 1895 was made in a nursery shed and a larger one in 1896 in the Katnook woolshed, with a trained winemaker in charge. After Riddoch's death in 1901 the property returned to sheep, and the woolshed went back to wool for decades. New vines were planted in 1971, and in 1980 the estate made its first commercial vintage of the modern era, again in the woolshed. Odyssey began with the 1991 vintage, held back and released in 1996 to mark a hundred years since the woolshed vintage of 1896; the name, the house says, stands for the estate's journey. Made only in years the house judges strong enough, from chosen rows of its own Cabernet, it stands beside a Shiraz, Prodigy, at the head of the range. Pour it as the wine that joins Riddoch's first Coonawarra vintages to the modern strip.

thirdPass.pushed: The Lynns had farmed around Penola for generations, as storekeepers and then graziers, when the family bought the property called Majella in 1960. In 1968 the sons of the family planted its first vines on the terra rossa, with their father's blessing, and from the 1970s they sold their grapes to the wineries of the district, Wynns among them. For two decades they were growers only. In 1991 they kept back enough Shiraz to make a wine of their own, made at the Brand family's Laira winery nearby, and the first Majella Shiraz was released. The Malleea followed with the 1996 vintage: Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz from the family's own vineyard, finished in new French oak and made only in years when the growing season suits it. The house glosses the name as an Aboriginal word for a green paddock, for the pastures of the Limestone Coast. The family later built its own winery on the farm. A guest who knows Coonawarra only for Cabernet meets its Shiraz here too, in a blend that turns a grower family's long knowledge of one vineyard into a label of its own.
